title: The PHP2Shell Postmortem: What CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 Actually Tell Us
summary:
I made a 6-minute video breakdown of this on YouTube — this is the written version for readers who prefer text. Same facts, same angles, better for linking in Slack or coming back to later.

On October 17, 2026 — four days before the patch shipped — AWS's MadPot honeypot caught something unusual: one HTTP request, no login, no session, no account. The server came back wrong.

Three days later, the CVE numbers for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 leaked on Hacker News, roughly 22 hours before the planned embargo lift. By the time PHP 8.5.12 / 8.4.27 / 8.3.36 / 8.2.35 went out, the exploit was already in the wild.

This post walks through four things I think are worth sitting with: the attack shape, the attacker fingerprint, the leak chain, and the 22-year pattern underneath. The video covers all of this visually; this is the "I want to re-read something while I'm waiting on a patch window" version.

title: 5 Common Security Mistakes in Python Scripts and How to Avoid Them
summary:
Python scripts are a powerful tool for automating tasks and building applications quickly. However, that convenience can also open doors to vulnerabilities if good security practices are not followed. Below we describe the five most frequent mistakes that appear in real‑world projects and offer practical recommendations to mitigate them.

1. Poor Exception Handling

Inadequate exception handling allows unexpected errors to leak to the user or cause the application to crash abruptly, exposing sensitive information such as system paths or stack traces. According to the article “Script Python revela errores de seguridad críticos”[^1], poor exception handling is one of the most common vulnerabilities.

title: Cisco ISE CVE-2026-20241 turns certificate issuance into an authorization decision
summary:
Cisco ISE CVE-2026-20241 turns certificate issuance into an authorization decision

Cisco published an authorization bypass in Identity Services Engine and the Passive Identity Connector on November 4, 2026. The advisory assigns CVE-2026-20241 a CVSS base score of 5.3 and says an unauthenticated, remote attacker can obtain an endpoint identity certificate. That description is short, but the operational consequence is larger than the certificate itself. ISE issues and validates credentials that network policy uses to decide whether an endpoint belongs on a network.

The advisory does not expose the vulnerable code path. It also lists no workarounds. Administrators should therefore avoid filling the gap with assumptions about the exact request or target API. What is confirmed is the security outcome: an endpoint certificate can be obtained without normal authorization. title: Three ways into a client's on-prem server, and where the client's switch sits
summary:
A government client's server is not my server. On-Prem Manager (OPM) can now reach one in three ways, so the useful question for each is who can turn it off.

OPM is the open-source tool I built to run on-premise Docker deployments: a cloud console, and one Go agent per server with its own GUI. Three things changed.

1. The browser tunnel is end-to-end encrypted

Some sites have no internet at all. For those, the agent borrows the browser of the person using its GUI: the tab fetches from the cloud on the agent's behalf.

Until this change, every request and response passed through that tab in clear. That included commits with secret values, and on a LAN the agent GUI may be plain http.

Now the agent seals each request to an X25519 key on the cloud, and that key has to be certified by a release key pinned in the agent's config. The cloud answers with an AES-256-GCM stream. The tab carries ciphertext.

title: 1,570 visitors, then a dead domain: what a registry-level suspension actually looks like
summary:

summary:

Enter the GPU cloud specialists: RunPod, Vast.ai, and Lambda Labs, all of which offer significantly cheaper GPU compute by leveraging spot pricing, community-owned hardware, or specialized infrastructure. But which one actually works for production AI inference?

🏆 RunPod is the best overall choice for indie developers deploying AI inference — it offers the most reliable serverless GPU experience with excellent tooling and reasonable pricing.

summary:

TL;DR ComfyUI generated a worried face for a clip that specified a neutral face. Multiple clips used the same image filename in input, so a later upload overwrote the file an earlier job was expected to read. Adding the episode ID and clip name to image and audio filenames prevents those collisions.

The conclusion first

The reason the video generated in ComfyUI with a neutral face specified ended up looking troubled was that multiple clips shared an image with the same filename, and a later image overwrote the file that an earlier job (the video-generation process) was reading. title: What AI agents actually need from infrastructure: 7 requirements, and where human-first hosting gets in the way
summary:
Most hosting was designed around a person at a keyboard: a sign-up form, a card, a dashboard, an email when something goes wrong. An AI agent that needs compute doesn't fit any of those steps. It can't solve a captcha, it can't tell a maintenance page from a broken one, and it won't notice that it has created the same server forty times.

It's tempting to say "just give it an API". That's the first requirement, not the last. Below are seven that we think matter, from building our own MCP server and REST API for agents. For each: what goes wrong without it.

1. Everything an agent needs is programmable
